questions.title: Chromosome content of primordial germ cells
questions.question: The primordial germ cells contain:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 23 double-strand chromosomes describes a haploid cell after DNA replication (e.g. a secondary spermatocyte/oocyte), not the diploid primordial germ cell.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 23 single-strand chromosomes would be a haploid, unreplicated cell -- primordial germ cells are diploid, not haploid.
explanations.C: Correct. Primordial germ cells (PGCs) are ordinary diploid cells, carrying the same somatic chromosome number as any other body cell: 46 single-strand (unreplicated) chromosomes. They arise in the wall of the yolk sac and migrate to the gonadal ridges, proliferating by ordinary mitosis before meiosis begins. Only after meiotic S-phase and the first meiotic division do their descendants become haploid, and only within meiotic prophase do their chromosomes carry duplicated (double-strand) chromatids.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 46 single chromosomes is a real, correct description (option C), so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.title: Meiotic stage of synapsis and crossing over
questions.question: Synapsis and crossing over occur in:

options.A: Prophase of the second meiotic division
options.C: Prophase of the first meiotic division

explanations.A: Incorrect. By the time meiosis II begins, homologous chromosomes are already segregated into haploid sets, so there are no longer homologous pairs available to synapse.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prophase of the first meiotic division is a real, correct answer (option C), so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.C: Correct. Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes, and crossing over is the reciprocal exchange of chromosomal segments between them; both take place during prophase of the first meiotic division (meiosis I), specifically within its pachytene sub-stage. Neither event occurs during prophase of meiosis II, since homologous pairs no longer exist by then. Mitotic prophase likewise involves no pairing of homologues, since mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells rather than the genetically varied gametes crossing over is for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mitotic prophase involves no pairing of homologous chromosomes at all, since mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells.

questions.title: Definition of ploidy
questions.question: Ploidy refers to:

options.A: Number of ribosomes in each cell
options.B: Amount of DNA in each cell
options.C: Number of chromosomes in each cell
options.D: Number of nuclei in each cell

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosome number is a measure of a cell's protein-synthetic machinery, unrelated to its chromosome number.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DNA amount changes with replication even when chromosome number does not -- a cell in G2 has double the DNA of a G1 cell at the same ploidy -- so ploidy and DNA content are not the same measurement.
explanations.C: Correct. Ploidy is the term for the number of complete chromosome sets, and by extension the number of chromosomes, present in a cell -- for example diploid (46, two sets) in somatic cells or haploid (23, one set) in mature gametes. It is not a measure of DNA content, ribosome number, or nuclear number, each of which is a separate cellular property. An abnormal ploidy state, such as triploidy or aneuploidy, is defined specifically by a change in chromosome number.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nuclear number (e.g. multinucleated cells such as osteoclasts or skeletal muscle fibres) is a separate cellular property from chromosome number.

questions.title: Chromosome number of gametes
questions.question: Gametes contain:

explanations.A: Correct. Mature gametes (the ovum and the spermatozoon) each carry a haploid number of chromosomes -- 23 in humans -- half the diploid somatic number of 46, produced by the two meiotic divisions. This halving is what restores the diploid number at fertilisation, when a haploid sperm and a haploid ovum fuse to form a diploid zygote. Gametes never carry the full diploid complement, and a haploid gamete still carries a full set of 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome, not merely a sex chromosome on its own.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The diploid number is the somatic cell number (46); gametes carry only the haploid number (23), produced by meiotic reduction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A haploid gamete carries a full haploid set -- 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome -- not merely a sex chromosome with no autosomes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Haploid number of chromosomes" (option A) is the correct answer, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.title: Stage of development at which implantation occurs
questions.question: At which stage of development does a fertilized ovum undergo implantation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. At the 4-cell stage the conceptus is still an early cleavage-stage embryo, well before it has differentiated into the structures implantation requires.
explanations.B: Correct. Implantation, the embedding of the conceptus into the endometrium, occurs once the conceptus has reached the blastocyst stage, roughly six days after fertilisation. The blastocyst is the first stage at which the conceptus has differentiated into an inner cell mass (the future embryo) and an outer trophoblast layer, whose outer syncytiotrophoblast is what actually invades the endometrial stroma. Neither the earlier cleavage stages nor the later gastrula stage (a post-implantation, second-to-third-week event) is when implantation itself begins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. At the 2-cell stage the zygote has only just begun cleaving, long before the trophoblast and inner cell mass needed for implantation exist.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gastrulation is a later, post-implantation event of the second-to-third week, not the stage at which implantation begins.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The morula is a solid ball of cells that has not yet formed the fluid-filled cavity and differentiated inner cell mass/trophoblast that define the blastocyst.

questions.title: Requirements for blastocyst implantation
questions.question: All of the following structures are necessary for blastocyst implantation EXCEPT?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A progestational (secretory-phase) endometrium is genuinely required -- it is the receptive state implantation depends on.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An intact functional layer of the endometrium is genuinely required, since this is the tissue the blastocyst invades.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Syncytiotrophoblast is genuinely required, since it is the invasive layer that actually erodes into the endometrial stroma.
explanations.D: Correct. The zona pellucida is required earlier in development -- to prevent polyspermy at fertilisation and to keep the dividing blastomeres from sticking prematurely to the tubal wall -- but it is shed ("hatching") before the blastocyst contacts the endometrium, so it plays no role in implantation itself. Implantation instead depends on a progestational, functionally active endometrium and a differentiated trophoblast providing both syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast. Listing the zona pellucida as a requirement for implantation reverses its actual developmental timing.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cytotrophoblast is genuinely required, since it underlies and continues to supply the invasive syncytiotrophoblast.

questions.title: Vignette: right-sided abdominal pain and bleeding after a missed period
questions.question: A 20-year old woman presents at the ER with severe abdominal pain on the right side with signs of abdominal bleeding. She indicated that she has been sexually active without contraception and missed her last menstrual period. Based on this information, which of the following disorders must be included as an option in the diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Appendicitis can cause right-sided abdominal pain but does not explain the missed period or the signs of abdominal (rather than gastrointestinal) bleeding described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A normal intrauterine pregnancy does not by itself cause severe abdominal pain and signs of abdominal bleeding; those findings point to a complication, not a normal course.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ovarian cancer would not typically present acutely with abdominal bleeding tied so specifically to a missed period in a young sexually active woman.
explanations.D: Correct. A missed menstrual period, unprotected sexual activity, and acute unilateral abdominal pain with signs of abdominal bleeding are the classic presentation of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Ectopic pregnancy is abnormal blastocyst implantation outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube; as the growing conceptus outstrips the tube's capacity, tubal rupture causes acute pain and can produce severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage. This combination of history and findings means ectopic pregnancy must be included in the differential diagnosis, even before further workup (such as a pregnancy test and ultrasound) confirms it.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Toxemia of pregnancy (pre-eclampsia) is a later-pregnancy hypertensive disorder, not an acute cause of abdominal pain and bleeding around the time of a missed period.

questions.title: Vignette: recurrent painless bleeding with a low-lying placenta
questions.question: A 26 year old woman experiences episodes of bright red vaginal bleeding at week 28, week 32 and week 34 of pregnancy. The bleeding spontaneously subsided each time. Using ultrasound, the placenta is located in the lower right portion of the uterus over the internal os. What is the diagnosis?

options.C: Premature rupture of the amniotic membrane

explanations.A: Correct. Placenta previa is placental implantation low in the uterus, near or over the internal cervical os. As the lower uterine segment stretches and thins in the third trimester, the placenta partially separates from it, producing the recurrent, painless, bright-red bleeding described here; the ultrasound finding of a placenta over the internal os confirms the diagnosis directly. This pattern -- self-limiting episodes recurring across the third trimester -- is the classic presentation this vignette is built around.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hydatidiform mole is a first-trimester gestational trophoblastic disease, not a third-trimester bleeding pattern with a normally formed, imaged placenta.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Premature rupture of membranes presents with fluid leakage, not recurrent painless bloody discharge, and does not by itself explain a low-lying placenta on ultrasound.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Toxemia of pregnancy (pre-eclampsia) presents with hypertension, proteinuria and oedema, not recurrent painless vaginal bleeding.

questions.title: Blastocyst component giving rise to the embryo
questions.question: What portion of the blastocyst will give rise to the embryo?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cytotrophoblast is part of the trophoblast, which forms the fetal contribution to the placenta and membranes, not the embryo proper.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Outer cell mass" is not a standard term for a distinct population at this stage; it is the trophoblast itself viewed from outside.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ectoderm does not yet exist at the blastocyst stage -- it differentiates later, from the inner cell mass, once it has organised into the bilaminar embryonic disc.
explanations.D: Correct. The blastocyst is organised into two populations: an outer trophoblast, which forms the fetal contribution to the placenta and fetal membranes, and an inner cell mass (embryoblast), a cluster of cells at one pole of the blastocyst cavity that gives rise to the embryo proper, including all three germ layers formed later at gastrulation. Neither ectoderm nor endoderm exists yet at this stage; both differentiate later from the inner cell mass.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endoderm, like ectoderm, does not yet exist at the blastocyst stage -- it differentiates later from the inner cell mass.

questions.title: First appearance of the amniotic cavity
questions.question: The amniotic cavity appears on the eighth day as a slit-like space between the trophoblast and the

explanations.A: Incorrect. The exocoelomic membrane forms slightly later, lining the primary yolk sac, and is not the second boundary of the day-eight amniotic cavity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The chorion is a later fetal membrane, formed by trophoblast plus extraembryonic mesoderm, not the structure bounding the amniotic cavity on day eight.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The connecting stalk develops slightly later as the link between the embryo and the developing placenta, not the day-eight boundary of the amniotic cavity.
explanations.D: Correct. On approximately the eighth day of development, a small, slit-like space appears within the inner cell mass, between the trophoblast and the embryoblast; this is the first appearance of the amniotic cavity. It is bounded, on the embryoblast side, by a single layer of cells called amnioblasts, which together with the adjacent epiblast will come to line the fully formed amniotic sac. This timing places the amniotic cavity's first appearance in the same narrow window as the trophoblast's differentiation into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Extraembryonic mesoderm appears later, filling the space between trophoblast and the exocoelomic/primary yolk sac membranes, not as the day-eight boundary of the amniotic cavity.

questions.title: Tissue origin of the chorion
questions.question: Chorion is formed by

explanations.A: Incorrect. This combines the wrong mesodermal layer (splanchnopleuric belongs to the yolk sac wall) with the wrong second tissue (hypoblast, not trophoblast).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Splanchnopleuric (visceral) mesoderm combines with extraembryonic endoderm to form the yolk sac wall, not with trophoblast to form the chorion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The mesoderm involved is extraembryonic, not intraembryonic -- intraembryonic mesoderm forms structures within the embryo proper, not the fetal membranes.
explanations.D: Correct. The chorion, the outermost fetal membrane and the fetal contribution to the placenta, is formed by the fusion of extraembryonic somatopleuric (somatic) mesoderm with the trophoblast (its cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast layers). This is in contrast to the amnion, formed by extraembryonic ectoderm plus somatopleuric mesoderm, and the yolk sac wall, formed by extraembryonic endoderm plus splanchnopleuric mesoderm. Naming the wrong mesodermal layer or the wrong second tissue is the standard distractor pattern for this fact.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Amnioblast" is not the tissue that fuses with somatopleuric mesoderm to form the chorion; amnioblasts instead line the amniotic cavity.

questions.title: Analyte detected by pregnancy tests
questions.question: Pregnancy tests generally are based upon the detection in maternal urine of

explanations.A: Incorrect. Oestrogen is a pregnancy-associated hormone but is not the analyte standard pregnancy tests detect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Human chorionic corticotropin" is not a real hormone -- a distractor built from a similar-sounding but non-existent name.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Human chorionic gonadotrophin (option E) is the correct answer, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Progesterone is a pregnancy-associated hormone but is not the analyte standard pregnancy tests detect.
explanations.E: Correct. Home and clinical pregnancy tests are generally based on detecting human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in maternal urine or serum. hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast from soon after implantation and is what maintains the corpus luteum -- and hence progesterone secretion -- until the placenta itself takes over steroid production. Oestrogen and progesterone are pregnancy hormones too, but neither is the analyte a standard pregnancy test detects.

questions.title: Connective tissue covering surrounding cartilage
questions.question: What is the connective tissue covering which surrounds cartilage?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Perimysium surrounds fascicles of skeletal muscle fibres, not cartilage.
explanations.B: Correct. The perichondrium is a two-layered fibrous capsule -- an outer fibrous layer rich in blood vessels and collagen-secreting fibroblasts, and an inner chondrogenic layer rich in chondroblasts -- that nourishes and grows cartilage. It surrounds hyaline and elastic cartilage but is absent at articular surfaces, which is exactly why articular cartilage has no independent blood supply route and instead depends on diffusion from synovial fluid. It is not surrounded by white fibrocartilage, which has no perichondrium at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Perineurium surrounds fascicles of nerve fibres within a peripheral nerve, not cartilage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Periosteum surrounds bone, not cartilage; it is the analogous covering for bone rather than cartilage.

questions.title: Cartilage type forming the tracheal rings
questions.question: What type of cartilage makes up the rings of the trachea?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Only hyaline cartilage forms the tracheal rings; elastic cartilage is not part of them.
explanations.B: Correct. Hyaline cartilage is the most common type of cartilage and the structural template for the other two types. It is found in the fetal skeleton, the articular surface of bones, costal cartilage, the epiphyseal plate, and the upper respiratory passages -- nose, larynx, trachea and bronchi -- which is exactly where the tracheal rings are located.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibrocartilage is a tough type found in sites such as the intervertebral disc and symphysis pubis, not the tracheal rings.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Elastic cartilage is found in the ear pinna, Eustachian tube, epiglottis and some laryngeal cartilages, not in the tracheal rings themselves.

questions.title: Cartilage type found in the external ear
questions.question: Which type of cartilage is found in the external ear?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither fibrocartilage nor hyaline cartilage is the type found in the external ear; that site is elastic cartilage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrocartilage sits in sites needing bone-to-bone attachment under stress, such as the intervertebral disc and symphysis pubis, not the external ear.
explanations.C: Correct. Yellow elastic cartilage is flexible and covered by perichondrium; it has the same structure as hyaline cartilage but with a large number of branching elastic fibres embedded in the matrix. It sits specifically in the ear pinna (external ear), the Eustachian tube, the epiglottis and some laryngeal cartilages, and the external auditory canal, giving it the flexibility to recover its shape after deformation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyaline cartilage sits in the fetal skeleton, articular surfaces, costal cartilage, the epiphyseal plate and the upper respiratory passages, not the external ear.

questions.title: Cartilage type forming the symphysis pubis
questions.question: Which type of cartilage forms the symphysis pubis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither elastic nor hyaline cartilage forms the symphysis pubis; that site is white fibrocartilage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Elastic cartilage sits in the ear pinna, Eustachian tube, epiglottis and larynx, not the symphysis pubis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyaline cartilage sits in the fetal skeleton, articular surfaces, costal cartilage, the epiphyseal plate and the upper respiratory passages, not the symphysis pubis.
explanations.D: Correct. White fibrocartilage is a tough type, important in bone-to-bone attachment, with characters intermediate between hyaline cartilage and dense regular white fibrous connective tissue; unlike hyaline and elastic cartilage, it has no perichondrium. It sits in the shoulder and hip joints, the intervertebral disc, the mandibular joint, the symphysis pubis, the sternoclavicular joint, and the semilunar cartilages of the knee -- sites needing strength and resistance to tensile stretch with limited mobility.

questions.title: Vignette: eroded articular cartilage with a narrowed joint space
questions.question: Mona is a fifty year-old female complaining of severe pain in her left knee joint. Plain X-ray of the joint showed erosion of the articular cartilage with marked reduction of the joint space and some other histopathological findings. What is the type of the articular cartilage?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Elastic fibrocartilage" is not a recognised cartilage type -- elastic cartilage and fibrocartilage are the two distinct, separate types this distractor combines.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Articular cartilage on a joint surface is hyaline, not fibrocartilage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Articular cartilage specifically lacks a perichondrium -- the one site where hyaline cartilage is not covered by one.
explanations.D: Correct. Hyaline cartilage is the most common type of cartilage, and the surface of a synovial joint such as the knee is covered by articular cartilage, which is hyaline cartilage without a perichondrium -- the one exception to the rule that a perichondrium surrounds hyaline cartilage. Its lack of a perichondrium means it has no independent blood supply and is nourished only by diffusion from synovial fluid, which is why degenerative erosion and narrowed joint space -- as in this vignette's osteoarthritis picture -- affect it so characteristically.

questions.title: Growth mode replacing worn cartilage near the articulating surface
questions.question: What is the normal mode of replacement of cells and matrix gradually worn away near the articulating surface of the cartilage?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Only interstitial growth replaces worn cells and matrix at the articulating surface itself; appositional growth adds new cartilage from the perichondrium instead, which is absent at articular surfaces.
explanations.B: Correct. The chondrocyte develops from the chondroblast, lies imprisoned in a lacuna, and divides into isogenous groups (clusters of 2 to 8 daughter cells within one lacuna) for interstitial growth -- growth from within the cartilage matrix itself. This is the mode by which cells and matrix gradually worn away near the articulating surface are replaced, since articular cartilage has no perichondrium to supply appositional growth from outside.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interstitial growth (option B) is the correct answer, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Appositional growth adds new cartilage from the chondrogenic layer of the perichondrium, which is specifically absent at articular surfaces -- so it cannot be the mode of replacement there.

questions.title: Bone cell responsible for initial matrix secretion and calcification
questions.question: Bone cell that is responsible for the initial secretion and calcification of the bone matrix is:

explanations.A: Correct. The osteoblast is the bone-forming cell. It arises from osteogenic (osteoprogenitor) cells and lies as a continuous single layer covering the bone surface under the periosteum and endosteum; by electron microscopy it shows the characters of a protein-forming cell -- abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and a well-developed Golgi apparatus -- consistent with its role secreting osteoid, which then becomes calcified. It is rich in alkaline phosphatase, the enzyme central to that calcification process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cell is the precursor that gives rise to the osteoblast; it does not itself actively secrete and calcify bone matrix.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The osteoclast resorbs bone matrix; it does not secrete or calcify it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The osteocyte is the mature, imprisoned bone cell that maintains matrix once formed, not the cell responsible for its initial secretion and calcification.

questions.title: Bone cell responsible for resorption
questions.question: Bone cell that is responsible for bone resorption is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The osteoblast secretes and calcifies new bone matrix; it does not resorb bone.
explanations.B: Correct. The osteoclast is a multinucleated cell formed by fusion of haemopoietic progenitors that resorbs bone from Howship's lacuna, the shallow pit its own resorptive activity creates on the bone surface. This resorptive function is the opposite of the osteoblast's matrix-forming role, and the two are balanced against each other in normal bone remodelling.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The osteocyte is the mature, imprisoned bone-maintaining cell, not a resorptive one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cell is a precursor that gives rise to osteoblasts, not a resorptive cell.

questions.title: Meaning of cancellous bone
questions.question: Cancellous bone means:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Woven (immature) bone is defined by its randomly oriented collagen fibres, a different classification axis from the compact/cancellous structural split.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Compact bone is the opposite structural category to cancellous bone -- built of Haversian systems with few marrow spaces, not a lattice of trabeculae.
explanations.C: Correct. Spongy (cancellous) bone is a lattice of irregular, branching and anastomosing bony trabeculae enclosing irregular bone marrow cavities, without Haversian systems, sited in the centre of flat, short and irregular bones and in the epiphyses of long bones. "Cancellous" and "spongy" are two names for this same structural category of bone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Dense bone" describes compact bone's appearance, the opposite structural category to cancellous (spongy) bone.

questions.title: Contents of Howship's lacunae
questions.question: The Howship's lacunae contain:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Osteoblasts occupy the bone surface as a continuous layer, not the resorption pits of Howship's lacunae.
explanations.B: Correct. The osteoclast is a multinucleated cell formed by fusion of haemopoietic progenitors that resorbs bone from Howship's lacuna. This lacuna is the shallow, scalloped resorption pit the osteoclast itself excavates as it degrades bone matrix, and it is where the cell characteristically sits. Its multinucleated, resorptive character contrasts directly with the single-nucleus, matrix-forming osteoblast.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The space of Disse is a perisinusoidal space in the liver, unrelated to bone resorption pits.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteocytes occupy their own individual lacunae distributed throughout calcified bone matrix, not the resorption pits specifically associated with osteoclasts.

questions.title: Alternative name for the Haversian system
questions.question: The Haversian system is also known as:

explanations.A: Correct. Compact bone is built of Haversian systems, each a canal with concentric lamellae, linked by Volkmann canals and interstitial lamellae. The Haversian system is also called the osteon, the structural unit of compact bone -- a cylindrical structure arranged parallel to the long axis of the bone, with a central Haversian canal carrying blood vessels and nerves, surrounded by 5 to 20 concentric circular bony lamellae with osteocytes in lacunae between them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Osteoid is the unmineralised organic bone matrix secreted by osteoblasts before it calcifies, not another name for the Haversian system.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The osteoblast is a bone cell, not a structural unit of compact bone architecture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The osteoclast is a bone cell, not a structural unit of compact bone architecture.

questions.title: First indicator of gastrulation
questions.question: The process of gastrulation is first indicated by the formation of the

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cloacal membrane is a bilaminar site formed by folding, not the structure that first indicates gastrulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The neural tube forms later, during neurulation (a fourth-week event), well after gastrulation has already begun.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The prechordal plate is a specialised area formed during gastrulation, not the first sign that gastrulation has begun.
explanations.D: Correct. Gastrulation is the transformation of the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar one, the characteristic event of the third gestational week. It begins with the formation of the primitive streak, a median narrow groove formed at the beginning of the third week by proliferation and migration of epiblast cells in the caudal epiblast. Epiblast cells then invaginate through this streak to form endoderm and, subsequently, the intraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.title: Site where the embryo remains bilaminar at gastrulation
questions.question: At gastrulation, the embryo is trilaminar except at:

explanations.B: Incorrect. Neural folds form later, during neurulation, from the already-trilaminar disc's ectoderm; they are not one of gastrulation's bilaminar exceptions.
explanations.C: Correct. Intraembryonic mesoderm is present between ectoderm and endoderm everywhere across the disc except at two sites: the buccopharyngeal membrane and the cloacal membrane, where ectoderm and endoderm remain fused with no mesoderm between them. The embryo therefore stays bilaminar specifically at the cloacal membrane (and the buccopharyngeal membrane) even after gastrulation has trilaminated the rest of the disc.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The primitive streak is the structure through which gastrulation begins, not a site where the disc remains bilaminar.

questions.title: Structural relations of the notochord
questions.question: The notochord is a ___ structure in vertebrate embryos that lies under the ___, and is flanked by ___.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The notochord lies under the neural tube specifically, not under "ectoderm" generally, and is flanked by the somites, not by endoderm.
explanations.B: Correct. The notochord is a mesodermal, rod-like structure that lies in the midline beneath the developing neural tube, with the paraxial mesoderm-derived somites flanking it on either side. This positional relationship -- ventral to the neural tube, between the two columns of somites -- is what lets the notochord induce overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate, and later provides the fixed axis around which the vertebral column condenses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The notochord is mesodermal, not endodermal, and its key relations are to the neural tube and somites, not to "the gut" in general.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The notochord is mesodermal, not endodermal, and "epidermis" and "blastocoel" are not its defining structural relations.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The notochord is classified as mesodermal, not ectodermal, once formed, even though it arises from epiblast cells that invaginate through the primitive node.

questions.title: Structure firmly attaching the chorion to the maternal endometrium
questions.question: During the formation of the placenta, it is important that the chorion firmly attaches to the maternal endometrial stroma. This is accomplished by the

explanations.A: Incorrect. Secondary chorionic villi are defined by developing a mesodermal core; they mediate villous growth, not the chorion's firm attachment to the endometrium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tertiary chorionic villi are defined by developing blood vessels within that mesodermal core, mediating maternal-fetal exchange, not firm anchoring.
explanations.C: Correct. Cytotrophoblast cells at the periphery of the chorionic villi proliferate and penetrate through the overlying syncytiotrophoblast to form a continuous outer layer, the outer cytotrophoblastic shell, which gradually surrounds the entire trophoblast. This shell is what firmly attaches the chorionic sac to the maternal endometrium, anchoring the developing placenta in place.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extraembryonic mesoderm forms the villous core (as part of secondary and tertiary villi), not the outer anchoring layer.

questions.title: Defining feature of secondary chorionic villi
questions.question: Chorionic villi are designated as secondary chorionic villi when they:

explanations.A: Correct. Chorionic villi progress through three stages: primary villi are columns of cytotrophoblast covered by syncytiotrophoblast, with no mesodermal core; they become secondary chorionic villi once extraembryonic mesoderm invades the cytotrophoblastic core; and they become tertiary (definitive) villi once blood vessels differentiate within that mesodermal core. It is specifically the appearance of the mesodermal core that marks the primary-to-secondary transition.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Contact with the decidua basalis is a positional relationship, not the defining structural change that marks the secondary stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Coverage by syncytiotrophoblast is already present from the primary villous stage, so it cannot be what newly defines the secondary stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Branching villi appear at a later stage of villous elaboration, not at the primary-to-secondary transition itself.

questions.title: Germ layer origin of the nervous system
questions.question: The nervous system is derived from?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endoderm gives rise to the gut epithelium and its budded derivatives, not the nervous system.
explanations.B: Correct. The central nervous system is a derivative of ectoderm: in the median plane of the ectoderm overlying the notochord, and induced by it, the cells thicken into the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube -- the whole central nervous system, grey and white matter alike. The peripheral nervous system, arising from the neural crest at the folds' crest, is likewise ectodermal in origin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Splanchnic mesoderm forms the connective tissue and musculature of the gut and its associated organs, not the nervous system.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesoderm in general forms connective tissues, muscle, the cardiovascular system and the urogenital system, not the nervous system.

questions.title: Name for the process forming the neural tube
questions.question: The process during which the neural tube begins to form is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Morulation" is not a standard embryological process term; it refers loosely to formation of the morula, an earlier cleavage-stage structure, not the neural tube.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Blastulation (formation of the blastocyst) is an earlier process, preceding gastrulation, not the process by which the neural tube forms.
explanations.C: Correct. Neurulation is the process by which the neural plate -- ectoderm thickened by the underlying notochord's inductive signal -- folds into the neural tube, the primordium of the central nervous system. The neural folds rise on either side of the neural groove, meet, and fuse to complete the tube. This process follows gastrulation and precedes the appearance of the neural crest as the folds fuse.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gastrulation is the earlier third-week process converting the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar one; it precedes, and sets up, neurulation but is not itself the tube-forming process.

questions.title: Facts concerning the neural folds
questions.question: Concerning neural folds:

options.A: They are induced to form by the underlying notochord
options.C: They join to form a tube that gives rise to the brain and spinal cord
options.D: They form during the third week of development

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own (though true). Induction by the underlying notochord is a genuine fact about neural folds, but it is not the only correct statement listed here, so "all of the above" is the fuller correct answer.
explanations.B: Correct. Every statement listed is true of the neural folds. The underlying notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, whose lips are the neural folds, and those folds then meet and fuse to form the neural tube, the primordium of the brain and spinal cord. This folding and fusion is a third-week event, immediately following gastrulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own (though true). That the folds join to form the neural tube giving rise to brain and spinal cord is genuine, but it is not the only correct statement listed here, so "all of the above" is the fuller correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own (though true). Third-week timing is genuine, but it is not the only correct statement listed here, so "all of the above" is the fuller correct answer.

questions.title: Timing of organogenesis
questions.question: Organogenesis occurs during:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Organogenesis is confined to the embryonic period, not the whole of pregnancy -- the fetal period that follows it is maturation and growth, not new organ formation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Second to sixth months describes part of the fetal period, when existing organs mature and grow, not the organ-forming embryonic period.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The first to second weeks span fertilisation through the bilaminar disc stage, before gastrulation has even produced the three germ layers organogenesis builds from.
explanations.D: Correct. The fetal period runs from the beginning of the 9th week -- the start of the 3rd month -- until birth, and is maturation and growth of already-formed tissues and organs rather than the formation of new ones. By definition, then, organogenesis -- the formation of organs -- occupies the embryonic period that precedes it: the third to the eighth week of development.

questions.title: Approximate day of cranial neuropore closure
questions.question: Closure of the cranial neuropore occurs at approximately:

explanations.A: Correct. As the neural folds fuse to form the neural tube, fusion begins in the cervical region and proceeds bidirectionally, leaving the cranial and caudal neuropores as the last points to close. The cranial neuropore closes at approximately day 25 of development, several days before the caudal neuropore. Failure of this cranial closure produces anencephaly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Day 15 is before neurulation itself has really got underway; the cranial neuropore has not yet formed, let alone closed, this early.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Day 30 is later than the cranial neuropore's actual closure, and would in fact postdate even the caudal neuropore's closure (~day 27-28).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Day 20 is slightly too early -- fusion of the neural folds is still progressing toward the cranial end at this point, before the cranial neuropore itself closes around day 25.

questions.title: Mechanism producing spina bifida
questions.question: Spina bifida occurs due to:

options.A: Failure of formation of the neural tube
options.B: Failure of closure of the caudal neuropore
options.D: Failure of closure of the cranial neuropore

explanations.A: Incorrect. The neural tube does form in spina bifida; it is specifically the caudal neuropore's closure, not tube formation itself, that fails.
explanations.B: Correct. Spina bifida is a neural tube defect of the vertebral column and spinal cord that results from failure of closure of the caudal neuropore, the temporary opening at the caudal end of the closing neural tube. This is distinct from anencephaly, which results from failure of closure of the cranial neuropore. Because the caudal neuropore normally closes at approximately day 27 to 28, a teratogenic or nutritional insult (such as folate deficiency) acting around this window is what most directly threatens its closure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Failure of closure of the caudal neuropore (option B) is the correct mechanism, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Failure of closure of the cranial neuropore produces anencephaly, not spina bifida.

questions.title: Timing of recognisable external body form
questions.question: The major features of the external body form are recognizable at:

options.A: The end of the eighth month
options.B: The end of the second month
options.C: The end of the sixth month
options.D: The end of the fourth month

explanations.A: Incorrect. By the end of the eighth month the fetus is already far into the fetal period's maturation and growth, long after the major features first became recognisable.
explanations.B: Correct. By the end of the second month (the end of the embryonic period proper, week 8), the major features of the external body form are already recognisable, even though the embryo remains only about 3 cm in crown-rump length: the head is large relative to the trunk, the face has taken on a more human appearance, and the limbs are formed with digits. This is distinct from the fetal period that follows, during which no new external features are laid down and existing ones instead mature and grow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By the end of the sixth month the fetus is well into the fetal period, refining features that were already recognisable months earlier.
explanations.D: Incorrect. By the end of the fourth month the fetus is already in the fetal period, past the point where these features first became recognisable at the end of the embryonic period.

questions.title: Ectodermal derivatives except one
questions.question: All of the following are derived from the ectoderm except:

options.D: The sensory epithelium of the ear, nose, and eye

explanations.A: Correct. Surface ectoderm and neuroectoderm together give rise to the central and peripheral nervous systems and the sensory epithelium of the ear, nose and eye. The kidneys, by contrast, are derived from intermediate mesoderm, not ectoderm -- the mesodermal odd-one-out in this otherwise ectodermal list. This same ectoderm/mesoderm boundary separates the ectodermal special sense organs from the mesodermal urogenital system throughout early development.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The central nervous system is genuinely ectodermal, arising from the neural tube.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The peripheral nervous system is genuinely ectodermal, arising largely from the neural crest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sensory epithelium of the ear, nose and eye is genuinely ectodermal, arising from surface ectoderm placodes.

questions.title: Neural crest derivatives except one
questions.question: All of the following are derived from the neural crest except

options.A: Parasympathetic ganglia of the gastrointestinal tract

explanations.A: Incorrect. Parasympathetic ganglia, including those of the gastrointestinal tract, are genuinely neural crest derivatives.
explanations.B: Correct. The neural crest, separating from the fusing neural folds, gives the sensory, sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, the Schwann cells, the melanocytes and the suprarenal medulla -- everything peripheral. The bones of the hand, by contrast, are mesodermal (limb bud mesenchyme) derivatives, not neural crest ones, making them the mesodermal exception in this otherwise neural-crest list.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The adrenal (suprarenal) medulla is genuinely a neural crest derivative -- crest cells migrate into the developing suprarenal cortex and differentiate into chromaffin cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Schwann cells, the peripheral myelinating glia, are genuinely a neural crest derivative.

questions.title: Germ layer origin of neural crest cells
questions.question: Neural crest cells are derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endoderm gives rise to gut epithelium and its budded derivatives, not the neural crest.
explanations.B: Correct. As the folds of the neural plate meet and fuse, cells at their crest separate as the neural crest and migrate widely; both the neural tube and the neural crest are ectodermal in origin, and neither gives rise to any mesodermal structure. The neural crest gives the sensory, sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, the Schwann cells, the melanocytes and the suprarenal medulla.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesoderm forms connective tissues, muscle and the cardiovascular/urogenital systems; the neural crest is ectodermal, not mesodermal, despite giving rise to some tissues (e.g. facial cartilage/bone) that are mesenchymal in character.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neural crest is specifically ectodermal in origin, not derived from all three germ layers.

questions.title: Neural crest derivatives except one (meninges)
questions.question: All of the following structures are derived from the neural crest except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glial cells of the peripheral nervous system (such as Schwann cells) are genuinely neural crest derivatives.
explanations.B: Correct. The neural crest gives rise to the sensory, sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes and the suprarenal medulla, and also contributes the arachnoid and pia mater (the leptomeninges). The dura mater, by contrast, is largely a mesodermal derivative (with a neural crest contribution only at the cranial vault), making it the exception this list singles out.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The arachnoid mater is genuinely a neural crest derivative, part of the leptomeninges.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pia mater is genuinely a neural crest derivative, part of the leptomeninges.

questions.title: Neural crest derivative among endocrine tissues
questions.question: Neural crest cells give rise to:

explanations.A: Correct. The neural crest gives rise to the sensory, sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, the Schwann cells, the melanocytes, and the suprarenal (adrenal) medulla. Neural crest cells migrate into the developing suprarenal cortex and differentiate there into the chromaffin cells of the medulla. This is why the medulla, unlike the cortex around it, is ectodermal (neural crest) rather than mesodermal in origin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pituitary gland has a dual origin from oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch, anterior lobe) and neuroectoderm of the diencephalon (posterior lobe), not from migrating neural crest cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pancreas is an endodermal derivative, budding from the foregut, not a neural crest derivative.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The adrenal cortex is a mesodermal derivative (from the intermediate mesoderm/coelomic epithelium region), the counterpart to the neural-crest-derived medulla it surrounds.

questions.title: Ectodermal derivatives except the upper anal canal
questions.question: Ectodermal derivatives include all of the following except:

options.A: Upper part of the anal canal

explanations.A: Correct. Surface ectoderm gives rise to the epidermis and its appendages (including the mammary gland), and neuroectoderm gives rise to the nervous system -- but the gastrointestinal tract, including the upper part of the anal canal above the pectinate line, is an endodermal derivative of the hindgut, not an ectodermal one. Only the lower part of the anal canal, below the pectinate line, is ectodermal, formed from the proctodeum, which is why the upper part is the exception in this otherwise-ectodermal list.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The mammary gland is genuinely a specialised ectodermal appendage, arising from the ectodermal mammary ridge.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The epidermis of the skin is genuinely the archetypal surface ectoderm derivative.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nervous system is genuinely a neuroectodermal derivative, via the neural tube and neural crest.

questions.title: Derivatives of intermediate mesoderm
questions.question: Intermediate mesoderm will give rise to the

explanations.A: Incorrect. The neural tube is a neuroectodermal derivative, not a mesodermal one at all.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Somites arise from paraxial mesoderm, a different mesodermal subdivision from intermediate mesoderm.
explanations.C: Correct. Intermediate mesoderm is the narrow strip connecting paraxial mesoderm to the lateral plate; it differentiates into the urogenital ridge, giving rise to the kidneys (via the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros) and the gonads. This is distinct from paraxial mesoderm (somites) and lateral plate mesoderm (body wall, limbs, cardiovascular system).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The heart arises from lateral plate (splanchnic) mesoderm, a different mesodermal subdivision from intermediate mesoderm.

questions.title: Somite derivatives except one
questions.question: Somites differentiate into all of the following except

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bone (vertebrae) is a genuine somite derivative, via the sclerotome.
explanations.B: Correct. Each somite splits into a sclerotome and a dermomyotome, and those become bone, dermis and muscle -- the sclerotome gives the vertebrae, and the dermomyotome splits further into a myotome (skeletal muscle) and a dermatome (dermis). The epidermis of the skin, by contrast, is a surface ectoderm derivative, not a somitic one, making it the exception in this list of somite-derived tissues.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Muscle (skeletal muscle of the trunk and limbs) is a genuine somite derivative, via the myotome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dermis of skin is a genuine somite derivative, via the dermatome -- distinct from the epidermis, which is ectodermal.

questions.title: Facts concerning somites
questions.question: Somites:

options.A: Differentiate into sclerotomes which give rise to vertebrae
options.B: Differentiate into myotomes which give rise to skeletal muscle in trunk and limbs
options.C: All of the above are correct
options.D: Arise from segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own (though true). Sclerotome formation of the vertebrae is genuine, but not the only correct statement listed, so "all of the above" is the fuller correct answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own (though true). Myotome formation of trunk/limb skeletal muscle is genuine, but not the only correct statement listed, so "all of the above" is the fuller correct answer.
explanations.C: Correct. Somites are the transverse segments of the paraxial mesoderm, arising by its segmentation on both sides of the notochord and neural tube. Each somite divides into a ventromedial sclerotome, whose cells migrate to surround the notochord and neural tube and form the vertebrae, and a dorsolateral dermomyotome, which subdivides into a dermatome (dermis) and a myotome (skeletal muscle of the trunk and limbs). All three listed statements -- sclerotome/vertebrae, myotome/muscle, and paraxial mesoderm origin -- are therefore correct together.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own (though true). Origin from segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm is genuine, but not the only correct statement listed, so "all of the above" is the fuller correct answer.

questions.title: Mesodermal derivatives except the suprarenal medulla
questions.question: The following organs are derived from mesoderm EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. Mesoderm gives rise to skeletal musculature (via somites), the smooth musculature of blood vessels, and the suprarenal cortex, among many other structures. The suprarenal medulla, by contrast, is a neural crest derivative -- neural crest cells migrate into the developing suprarenal cortex and differentiate into chromaffin cells -- so it is the one structure in this list that is ectodermal in origin rather than mesodermal, despite sitting inside a mesoderm-derived organ.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Skeletal musculature is genuinely a mesodermal derivative, via the myotomes of the somites.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The suprarenal cortex is genuinely a mesodermal derivative, the counterpart to the neural-crest-derived medulla it surrounds.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The musculature (smooth muscle wall) of blood vessels is genuinely a mesodermal derivative.

questions.title: Total number of somites
questions.question: The whole number of somites is

explanations.A: Correct. Somites, the paired segmental blocks of paraxial mesoderm, appear in craniocaudal sequence through the fourth and fifth weeks and total approximately 42 to 44 pairs by the end of somite formation. This is considerably more than the roughly 30 to 35 vertebrae that persist in the adult axial skeleton. Several of the most caudal somites subsequently regress, which is why the final vertebral count is smaller than the total number of somites ever formed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 46 to 48 overstates the total somite count; the correct total is approximately 42 to 44 pairs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 30 to 35 is closer to the final adult vertebral count, not the total number of somites ever formed, several of which regress.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 36 to 40 understates the total somite count; the correct total is approximately 42 to 44 pairs.

questions.title: Germ layer derivative of the vertebral column
questions.question: The vertebral column is derived from

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lateral plate mesoderm forms the body wall, limbs and serous cavity linings, not the vertebral column.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The dermomyotome, the other half of a differentiated somite, forms the dermis and skeletal muscle, not the vertebrae.
explanations.C: Correct. Each somite splits into a ventromedial sclerotome and a dorsolateral dermomyotome. The sclerotome cells migrate medially to surround the notochord and neural tube and form the vertebrae and intervertebral discs, which is why the vertebral column is described as derived from the sclerotomes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intermediate mesoderm forms the kidneys and gonads, not the vertebral column.

questions.title: Timing of embryonic folding
questions.question: Folding of the embryo occurs during:

explanations.A: Correct. Cephalocaudal and lateral folding converts the flat trilaminar embryonic disc into a cylindrical, tube-within-a-tube body, with the amniotic cavity surrounding it and the yolk sac partly incorporated as the primitive gut. This folding takes place during the fourth week of development. It is the same week in which somites, the neural tube and the first pharyngeal arches are also forming.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The third week is when gastrulation forms the trilaminar disc that folding subsequently acts on, not when folding itself occurs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By the sixth week, folding is long complete and the embryo already has its basic body form; folding itself is a fourth-week event.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The second week is the implantation/bilaminar-disc period, well before the trilaminar disc that folding requires even exists.

questions.title: Midgut communication with the yolk sac
questions.question: The midgut communicates with the yolk sac by

explanations.A: Incorrect. The allantois runs through the connecting stalk toward the hindgut/cloacal region and contributes to bladder development, not the midgut-yolk sac connection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cloacal membrane is a bilaminar site at the caudal end of the disc, not a communicating duct between midgut and yolk sac.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The oropharyngeal (buccopharyngeal) membrane is a bilaminar site at the cranial end of the disc, not a communicating duct between midgut and yolk sac.
explanations.D: Correct. Once the embryo folds and the dorsal part of the yolk sac is incorporated into the embryo as the primitive gut tube, the midgut remains in open communication with the remaining, extraembryonic part of the yolk sac through a narrow connecting channel: the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, which runs through the umbilical cord. The duct normally obliterates later in development; its persistence is the embryological basis of Meckel's diverticulum.
